questions.question: A double bar graph shows how many students in two classes chose soccer at recess. The scale is 1 student for each grid line. The bar for Division 4 reaches 8 and the bar for Division 5 reaches 5. How many more students in Division 4 chose soccer?
questions.explain: To compare two bars in a double bar graph, subtract the shorter value from the taller one: 8 - 5 = 3. A common trap is adding the two bars (8 + 5 = 13), but 'how many more' always means subtract.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows winter activities chosen by two classes, with a scale of 1 student per grid line. Skating: Division 4 reaches 12, Division 5 reaches 9. Swimming: Division 4 reaches 11, Division 5 reaches 5. Hiking: Division 4 reaches 7, Division 5 reaches 5. Which activity has the biggest difference between the two classes?
questions.explain: Find each pair's difference: skating 12 - 9 = 3, swimming 11 - 5 = 6, hiking 7 - 5 = 2, so swimming has the biggest gap. The trap is choosing skating because it has the single tallest bar — the tallest bar is not the same as the biggest difference.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows club sign-ups in two classes, scale 1 student per grid line. Art: Division 4 reaches 7, Division 5 reaches 9. Drama: Division 4 reaches 6, Division 5 reaches 10. Dance: Division 4 reaches 9, Division 5 reaches 7. Music: Division 4 reaches 8, Division 5 reaches 8. In which club did the two classes sign up exactly the same number of students?
questions.explain: The two bars are equal only when both classes have the same number, and that happens in music (8 and 8). Every club here has a total of 16, so a common trap is picking one because the totals match — equal bars means the two values themselves are the same.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows fruit brought for snack in two classes, scale 1 student per grid line. Apples: Division 4 reaches 9, Division 5 reaches 6. Oranges: Division 4 reaches 4, Division 5 reaches 7. Bananas: Division 4 reaches 8, Division 5 reaches 3. Grapes: Division 4 reaches 10, Division 5 reaches 5. For which fruit did Division 5 bring MORE than Division 4?
questions.explain: Check each pair and see where the Division 5 value is larger: only oranges, where 7 is greater than 4. The trap is grabbing the biggest number on the graph (grapes, 10) instead of watching which class the question is asking about.

questions.question: At a Surrey school, a double bar graph shows how many students walk to school in each grade. The scale is 5 students for each grid line. The Grade 4 bar reaches 4 grid lines and the Grade 5 bar reaches 7 grid lines. How many more Grade 5 students walk to school?
questions.explain: With a many-to-one scale, change grid lines into students first: 7 x 5 = 35 and 4 x 5 = 20, so 35 - 20 = 15. The most common trap is subtracting the grid lines (7 - 4 = 3) and forgetting that each line stands for 5 students.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows money raised at a Kelowna school bake sale, with a scale of $10 for each grid line. Cookies: Saturday reaches 6 lines, Sunday reaches 4 lines. Muffins: Saturday reaches 3 lines, Sunday reaches 5 lines. Over the two days together, how much more did cookies raise than muffins?
questions.explain: Total each item over both days first: cookies $60 + $40 = $100 and muffins $30 + $50 = $80, so the difference is $20. A common trap is comparing only Saturday ($60 - $30 = $30) instead of using both days.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows snowfall on two BC mountains, with a scale of 2 cm for each grid line. Monday: Cypress 5 lines, Grouse 3 lines. Tuesday: Cypress 4 lines, Grouse 6 lines. Wednesday: Cypress 7 lines, Grouse 2 lines. Thursday: Cypress 3 lines, Grouse 6 lines. On which day did the two mountains get the greatest snowfall altogether?
questions.explain: Add the pair for each day (in grid lines is enough since the scale is the same): Monday 8, Tuesday 10, Wednesday 9, Thursday 9, so Tuesday is greatest at 10 x 2 = 20 cm. The trap is picking Wednesday because it has the tallest single bar.

questions.question: A double bar graph at the Burnaby library shows books borrowed, with a scale of 4 books for each grid line. Fiction: Monday 5 lines, Tuesday 3 lines. Non-fiction: Monday 2 lines, Tuesday 6 lines. How many books in total were borrowed on Tuesday?
questions.explain: Multiply each Tuesday bar by the scale, then add: 3 x 4 = 12 fiction and 6 x 4 = 24 non-fiction, so 12 + 24 = 36 books. The trap is adding the grid lines (3 + 6 = 9) without using the scale of 4.

questions.question: Two divisions ran a food-drive at a Victoria school. On the double bar graph the scale is 5 cans for each grid line. The Division 4 bar reaches 6 grid lines and the Division 5 bar reaches 10 grid lines. Aanya says, 'Division 5 collected 4 more cans, because its bar is 4 squares taller.' How many more cans did Division 5 actually collect?
questions.explain: Squares are not cans: 10 x 5 = 50 and 6 x 5 = 30, so Division 5 collected 50 - 30 = 20 more cans. Aanya made the most common many-to-one mistake — counting the 4 extra squares instead of multiplying that gap by the scale of 5.

questions.question: A Nanaimo pool made a double bar graph of swim passes sold in April and May, scale 5 passes per grid line. Children: April 5 lines, May 9 lines. Adults: April 6 lines, May 9 lines. How many more did the children's passes increase from April to May than the adults' passes did?
options: 0 — both groups ended at the same number
questions.explain: Find each group's increase first: children 45 - 25 = 20 and adults 45 - 30 = 15, so children increased 5 more. The trap is comparing the May bars, which are equal, instead of comparing how much each group changed.

questions.question: Two Grade 5 classes tracked reading. On the double bar graph the scale is 10 minutes for each grid line. Division 6: Monday 4 lines, Tuesday 6 lines, Wednesday 5 lines. Division 7: Monday 6 lines, Tuesday 3 lines, Wednesday 7 lines. Over the three days, which class read more, and by how much?
options: The two classes read the same amount
questions.explain: Add each class across all three days, then use the scale: Division 6 has 15 lines = 150 minutes and Division 7 has 16 lines = 160 minutes, so Division 7 read 10 minutes more. The trap is answering 1 minute, which is the gap in grid lines before multiplying by 10.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows pets owned by two classes, scale 1 pet per grid line. Division 3: dogs 8, cats 6, fish 4. Division 4: dogs 5, cats 9, fish 4. Which statement does this double bar graph support?
options: Fish are the most popular pet in Division 4.
Division 3 owns more of every kind of pet than Division 4.
The two classes own the same number of dogs.
Division 4 owns 3 more cats than Division 3.
questions.explain: Test each claim against the pairs of bars: cats are 9 and 6, so Division 4 owns exactly 3 more. The trap is assuming that because Division 3 leads in dogs it leads everywhere — on a double bar graph you must check each category separately.
